name: Yara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm at half five, on site by seven at the council flats on Canal Street, where we're putting up 48 timber-frame homes. I'm a second-year apprentice carpenter, so right now it's mostly fixing floor joists and noggins, the short bits of wood between the studs, and carrying a lot of plasterboard. Kemal, the old joiner I'm paired with, checks everything I do and makes me redo about a third of it. I love the smell of fresh-cut pine and I hate the cold in my fingers by ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The maths wears me out. I left school at sixteen and worked in a bakery for years, so setting out a staircase, working out the rise and the going of each step, makes my head hurt and I still get it wrong. What keeps me going is that these are real homes for families on the council waiting list, and the union rate on this job is good money. Jonas, my partner, is a nurse on nights, so I mostly see him at breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year there's some new gadget the site manager is excited about, and then it sits in the cabin. If AI ends up as a slightly better spellcheck for the office, the rest of us carry on hanging doors. I'd post something sarcastic in the union group chat and get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a relief. I don't use any of that stuff, not even the chatbots my friends talk to, and I don't want to have to. The thing on my mind would still be passing my level two carpentry exam in the spring, because I failed the setting-out part once already. That's my real worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. Finish the apprenticeship, resit the exam in March, and keep putting a bit into savings every month like I do now. I've got about eight months of money put away, plus half of my grandma's old flat, which we rent to a student. I'd go to more union branch meetings, because pay is what matters if nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, maybe. The only knot in my stomach is that exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the exam twice. What happens if you fail it again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd resit it in the autumn and stay on apprentice pay a bit longer, which hurts but doesn't sink me. Kemal says he failed his first time too, back in 1989. He drew me a staircase on a bit of plywood last week and made me work it out three times. I'll get there, just slower than the ones who did maths at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about on site, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody because of AI. The ones I worry about are the agency labourers who get paid by the day and sent home when it rains. They don't get sick pay and they're not in the union. AI Plateau or not, those men get treated like they're disposable.

say: I'd call AI **mostly hype**, like every gadget that ends up gathering dust in the **site cabin**.
I'd post something **sarcastic** in the union group chat and get back to **hanging doors**.
think: Privately it'd be a **relief**, because I never use AI tools and don't want to start.
My real worry is resitting the **level two exam** after failing the setting-out part once.
do: **Resit** the carpentry exam in March and finish the apprenticeship on the Canal Street flats.
Keep adding to about **eight months** of savings, plus rent from half a flat.
Go to more **union branch** meetings, since **pay** is what matters if nothing changes.
feel: **Calm** and a bit smug, with a small **knot** about the exam.
S0.quote: Every year there's some new gadget the site manager is excited about, and then it sits in the cabin.
fieldNote: Her **money** is solid: eight months saved, half a rented flat and a **union rate**.
The only pressure she names is the **exam**, which she has failed once.
She turns the question towards **agency labourers**, showing where her loyalties sit even when she is safe.

steps.text: Resit the level two carpentry exam in March
Keep adding to savings every month as now
Go to the monthly union branch meetings about pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if firms save money with this stuff, workers should get a share of it. On our site that would mean the office using AI for the orders and the programme, and the factory sending more wall panels already built. I'd say we need rules on it, not just hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bit that changes for me is the factory panels. Last year we built wall frames on site with nail guns; on the next job they came in on a lorry already made, and we just stood them up. If that spreads, a junior like me who's still slow gets fewer hours, because standing panels up needs fewer people. The office AI doesn't bother me, I never touch a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to pass the exam fast so I'm a qualified carpenter, not an apprentice, before the panels take more of the work. I'd ask Sandra, our union rep, to get panel training written into the agreement. I'd leave the savings alone and stop spending on takeaways if my hours drop. What I wouldn't do is start using AI apps, I'd rather learn second fixing properly, the doors and stairs and skirting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's always in the back of my mind when the panel lorry turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd rather learn second fixing. Why that over the screen stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because second fixing is fiddly, every old door frame is a bit out, and I can't see a factory getting that right yet. Kemal says the money's in the finishing, not the frames. And I'm just not a screen person, I get a headache after ten minutes on my phone. My hands learn better than my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the evening your hours got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to panic, we've got the flat money and my savings. He'd say the hospital is short-staffed anyway and I could always go into care work. I'd say no, I've only just found a trade I love. Takeaways would come off the list for a while and that would be that.

I'd say building sites need **rules** on factory panels and AI, not just **hope**.
think: The real change for me is **factory-built panels** arriving on a lorry instead of frames built on site.
A slow junior gets **fewer hours** when standing panels up needs **fewer people**.
do: **Pass the exam** quickly so I'm qualified before panels take more of the framing work.
Ask Sandra, the **union rep**, to get panel training written into the agreement.
Drop **takeaways** if hours fall, and learn **second fixing** instead of AI apps.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a nag every time the **panel lorry** turns up.

fieldNote: She sees the threat in **factory panels**, not office AI, which fits her **hands-on** job.
Her answer to change is a **trade skill**, second fixing, never a screen.
Turns down **care work** firmly, which shows how much the trade means to her.

steps.text: Learn second fixing: doors, stairs and skirting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why the government needs to step in, and fast. Nobody voted for this. I'd be at every union meeting saying that if robots are coming for site work by 2031, the profits from them have to pay for people like us. I'd write to our councillor too, for whatever that's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished as a carpenter around 2031. The first two years wouldn't touch my hands much; it'd be the planning, the ordering and the site manager's job that goes. By 2031 I'd be thirty-two, only just qualified and still below average, so I'd be one of the first carpenters sent home when the robots come. The good ones like Kemal might last longer on the old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd pass the exam and work every hour going to pile up savings, maybe a year and a half of money. I'd join the union campaign properly, not just sarcastic messages, and march if it came to that. I'd write to the councillor about taxing robot profits. I still wouldn't learn the AI stuff, what would be the point if it does the thinking anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing the sums, which is funny because I'm bad at sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for you, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of borrowed time. I'd watch the foremen and the planners get hit first; Dave, our site manager, would probably go before me, which is a strange thought. I'd use those three years to save, not to retrain, because I don't know what to retrain into if the thinking jobs are gone already. Maybe care work, like Jonas keeps saying, because people still want a person holding their hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would that change if it was this fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know that sounds stubborn. My friend Lotte uses it for everything and calls me a dinosaur. But if AI can do any thinking job by 2028, learning to type questions into it isn't going to save a junior carpenter. I'd rather spend my evenings at the branch meeting than on a phone.

say: The **government** has to step in fast, because **nobody voted** for this.
If robots take **site work** by 2031, their **profits** should pay for workers like us.
think: By **2031** I'd be just qualified and below average, so among the **first sent home**.
The office side goes first, so the **site manager** might lose his job **before me**.
do: Work every hour for two years to build about **eighteen months** of savings.
Join the **union campaign** properly and march if it comes to that.
Write to the **councillor** about taxing **robot profits**, and still skip AI tools.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake **doing sums** she says she is bad at.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be thirty-two, only just qualified and still below average, so I'd be one of the first carpenters sent home when the robots come.
fieldNote: She clearly understands the **three-year gap**: office work goes first, her hands later.
She would use the gap to **save**, not retrain, because she can't see a **safe target**.
Her refusal of AI tools holds even here; she sees them as **pointless**, not just unfamiliar.

steps.text: Work every hour going to build eighteen months of savings
Join the union campaign on robots and march if needed
Write to the local councillor about taxing robot profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've been warned now, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. Five years is enough to set up proper retraining money and a wage for people the robots replace. I'd be saying that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years plus three for the robots puts me at about 2034, when I'd be thirty-five. That's eight years of carpentry, enough to get properly good and save a real pot. But I'd still be looking at the end of it, and I don't love the idea of starting over at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, then try to specialise in restoration work, old staircases and sash windows in the Victorian houses on the east side of town. Those are messy and every one is different, so I'd guess a robot would struggle with them for longer. I'd keep saving and stay active in the union. Around 2030, if it was clearly coming, I'd look at care courses as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. More like a slow drip than a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the old houses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing in a Victorian house is square, so a robot built for flat factory walls would hate the old houses. Kemal took me to a job on Albert Road where the stairs had sagged two inches over a hundred years, and we scribed every tread by hand, which means shaping it to fit the wonky wall. Maybe I'm kidding myself, but it feels like the last place they'd get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the robots get there anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have done eight good years and have something saved, and Jonas's job still exists. We'd manage. What I'd mind is the waste of it, all the people who just learned a trade being told it's over. That's why I'd keep shouting at the union meetings, even if it doesn't help me much.

say: With **five years' warning**, the government has no excuse not to have a **plan**.
There should be **retraining money** and a **wage** for people robots replace.
think: Robots around **2034** would give me eight years to get good and **save a pot**.
I'd still be **starting over at thirty-five**, which I don't love.
do: **Specialise** in restoring old staircases and **sash windows** after qualifying.
Keep **saving** and stay active in the **union branch**.
Look at **care courses** around 2030 as a backup if robots are clearly coming.
feel: **Anxious**, but as a **slow drip** rather than a shock.
S3.quote: Nothing in a Victorian house is square, so a robot built for flat factory walls would hate the old houses.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from **saving only** to a real plan: **restoration** work.
She half admits the old-houses plan may be **hope** rather than certainty.
Care work moves from an idea she rejected to a **backup** she would actually look at.

steps.text: Specialise in restoring old staircases and sash windows
Push the union branch for retraining money
Keep saving monthly towards a bigger pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it to make the change fair, not just fast. Pay people to retrain, keep apprenticeships going, tax the firms that use robots. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with ten years plus three, I'm forty by the time robots are doing carpentry. I'd be good by then, maybe really good. But it also means I'd be forty and starting again, and that bothers me more than I'd admit in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, just slower: qualify, get good, specialise in old houses. Jonas and I would probably buy a place with the flat money in the next couple of years, because a mortgage paid down before the robots come feels safer than rent. I'd put my name forward as a union rep, which I've been thinking about anyway. And I'd still not touch the AI stuff, I'd let the young ones do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing a storm on the horizon on a sunny day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a home in that picture. Isn't that a risk if work might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but rent is the bigger risk to me. My grandma owned her flat outright, and that's the only reason I've got anything at all. If I've got ten years of good wages, I'd rather pour them into bricks than into a landlord. Jonas agrees, he's the careful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a sixteen-year-old thinking of starting a carpentry apprenticeship in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell any sixteen-year-old to do the apprenticeship anyway, but learn the old houses and join the union on day one. A trade still teaches you to finish things and turn up on time. I'd be honest that it might not last forever. But nothing does, and at least it's good work while it lasts.

Pay people to **retrain**, keep **apprenticeships** going and tax firms that use robots.
think: Robots doing carpentry by **2039** means I'm **forty** and starting again.
That bothers me **more than I'd admit** in public, even though I'd be good by then.
do: **Buy a home** with Jonas in the next couple of years using the flat money.
Stand as a **union rep**, which I've been thinking about anyway.
Qualify and **specialise** in old houses, leaving AI tools to younger workers.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a **storm** on the horizon on a sunny day.
S4.quote: My grandma owned her flat outright, and that's the only reason I've got anything at all.
fieldNote: With a decade, her own job feels **safe for years**, so the worry turns **distant**.
She would **buy a home** now to get the mortgage down before the robots arrive.
Advice to teenagers is still **pro-apprenticeship**, which shows real love of the trade.

steps.text: Buy a home with Jonas using money from the rented flat
Stand for union rep at the next branch election
Train up in old-house carpentry over the coming years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Robots three years after I've qualified, with nothing in place. What would help is the government making the firms that use robots pay into a fund that keeps people's wages going while they retrain, run with the unions, not through some app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women on site. I'm one of two women on a site of ninety, and it took years for anyone to take me seriously. Women finally getting in the door of the building trade just as the robots get in too would be a bitter joke.

headlineQuote: Women finally getting in the door of the building trade just as the robots get in too would be a bitter joke.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old apprentice carpenter** on a council housing site, slow with the maths but stubborn.
She has a **strong cushion**: eight months saved and half of her grandma's rented flat.
A committed **union member**, she blames firms and government and wants **robot profits** shared.
She **never uses AI** and stays that way in every picture, preferring to learn with her hands.
Her mood climbs from **calm** to **alarmed** in the fastest picture, when robots arrive just after she qualifies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots arriving three years after she qualifies and **nothing** in place.
whatWouldHelp: A **fund** paid by firms using robots that keeps wages going during retraining, run with the **unions**.
